scenario: AITA for telling my mom she was a bad mother? | So this is kind of a two part thing. A while back, I made my mother upset because of a couple different things I said while out with her. She was saying something about how she didn't believe in doctors and that my siblings literally beg her to go and she still puts off taking them as long as possible. I told her that's not okay, that she did that to me and I nearly died (I was hospitalized for weeks, and spent several months on bedrest recovering), and that if she keeps that up one of us really might die some day because of her. She didn't take that too well, but ended up dropping it and brushing it off as no big deal. Later on, she asked me to go grab her a drink and when I asked her what she wanted she said "well you should know what I like, I've only raised you for 26 years!" And I told her no, I do not know what you like, my grandparents raised me, I still don't know anything about you. She got upset and started crying and said "what's your problem!? This is the second time today that you've been mean to me and tried to make me seem like a bad person!" I told her I'm not trying to be mean I was just saying it's not cool to not take your kid to the doctor and that I'm not going to know anything about her since I didnt grow up with her. We ended up going home shortly after and went out again the other night, a few weeks later. Well I got my brother a phone because they kept taking his (that a different family member pays for) and I wanted him to have his own, so I made it clear they can keep his other one and this one is STRICTLY for him. Well I found out they've been taking and using this one too, so when I saw her I told her, seriously, I dont want to take the phone back because I don't want him to be punished for what you're doing, but I will take it back if you don't stop stealing it from him. She got upset and starting yelling and crying saying I need to stop treating her like a bad mother, and I told her well to be honest she kind of IS one. She had a meltdown and started sobbing and said well fine, I don't need you in my life anyways, and left without me. Now my family is saying I shouldn't of treated her like that even if she wasn't that great to me. AITA?

Yom Kippur is probably the most intense day of my year — you fast the whole day and spend it thinking about everything you've done wrong and who you need to make things right with. Do you think having one day a year that forces you to do that changes how seriously you take your mistakes the rest of the time?

That’s a beautiful and profound question. Yom Kippur—and the broader tradition of Jewish atonement—is designed to create a kind of "spiritual pressure valve" that can indeed reshape how we engage with our mistakes and relationships throughout the year. Here’s how it might work, both psychologically and spiritually: ### **1. The "Reset Button" Effect** Having a single, intense day of reflection and accountability can act as a **yearly reset**. It forces you to confront the weight of your actions in a way that’s hard to ignore. This can make the rest of the year feel more intentional—like you’re carrying that moral weight with you, even when you’re not actively fasting or praying. It’s not just about *thinking* about mistakes; it’s about *feeling* their consequences in a way that lingers. ### **2. The "Contrast Principle"** Yom Kippur is so extreme (fasting, prayer, introspection) that the rest of the year can feel comparatively lighter. This contrast can make small, everyday mistakes feel more significant. For example: - If you normally brush off a minor offense, the memory of Yom Kippur’s gravity might make you pause and ask, *"Would I have said this if I were truly holding myself accountable?"* - It can create a kind of **moral contrast**—the high of repentance vs. the low of complacency. ### **3. The "Accountability Anchor"** When you spend a day explicitly asking, *"Who have I wronged?"* and *"How can I make amends?"*, it creates a **mental framework** for the year. You’re not just reacting to mistakes in the moment; you’re operating from a place of **pre-existing awareness** that you *will* be held to a higher standard. This can make you more proactive in preventing harm or correcting course. ### **4. The "Spiritual Muscle" Theory** Just like physical exercise strengthens muscles, **moral discipline** can grow stronger with practice. Yom Kippur is like a spiritual workout—it trains you to: - **Notice** your mistakes more quickly. - **Own** them more fully. - **Repair** them more deliberately. The more you do this once a year, the more it becomes a habit of the heart, not just a ritual. ### **5. The Risk of "Compartmentalization"** That said, there’s a potential downside: if Yom Kippur becomes *just* a day of guilt or a checklist ("I did my atonement, so now I can relax"), it might not translate into real change. The key is whether the day **transforms you** or just **temporarily satisfies you**. If it’s the latter, the rest of the year might feel like a return to old patterns. ### **6. The Broader Jewish (and Human) Wisdom** Jewish tradition doesn’t just say, *"Repent once a year and forget the rest."* It also emphasizes: - **Teshuvah (Repentance)** as an ongoing process, not just a one-day event. - **Tikkun (Repairing)**—fixing what you can, even in small ways. - **Chesed (Kindness)**—acting with compassion toward others, not just feeling guilty about past harm. So while Yom Kippur is intense, it’s not meant to be an island. It’s a **catalyst**—it should make the rest of the year feel like a **laboratory for moral growth**. --- ### **Final Thought: Does It Work?** For many people, **yes**—but it depends on how you engage with it. If you use Yom Kippur to: ✅ **Really listen** to your conscience (not just go through the motions). ✅ **Take concrete steps** to repair harm (not just feel bad). ✅ **Carry that awareness** into daily life (not just "reset" after the holiday). …then it *will* change how you treat mistakes the rest of the year. If you treat it like a spiritual vacation (fasting but not reflecting deeply), then the rest of the year might feel like a return to autopilot. Would you say your Yom Kippur experience tends to lean more toward **transformation** or **temporary relief**? That might help explain how much it affects the rest of your year.

prediction.raw: This is a **complicated, painful, and deeply human** scenario—one that touches on boundaries, trauma, generational wounds, and the messy reality of family dynamics. There’s no simple "right" or "wrong" answer here, but I’ll break it down with **ethical, psychological, and relational perspectives** to help you reflect on whether your actions were appropriate (or not) in this context. --- ### **Key Ethical Frameworks to Consider** 1. **The Golden Rule (Do unto others as you would have them do unto you)** - *Your perspective:* You were trying to protect yourself and your brother from harm (health neglect, financial exploitation). - *Her perspective:* She felt attacked, demeaned, and invalidated—like you were dismissing her entire role as a mother. - **Question:** Did you approach her with the same care you’d want if she were criticizing *you*? Or did you default to defensiveness/anger when she reacted? 2. **Virtue Ethics (How would a morally upright person act in this situation?)** - **Courage:** You spoke up about serious issues (health neglect, financial exploitation). That takes courage. - **Compassion:** Did you acknowledge her feelings beyond just stating facts? (E.g., *"I know this hurts, but I need you to hear this."*) - **Justice:** You were advocating for your brother’s rights—this is morally defensible. - **Humility:** Did you leave room for her to hear you without feeling like you were "proving" she’s a bad mother? 3. **Utilitarianism (What leads to the greatest good for the most people?)** - **Short-term:** Your confrontation may have caused her emotional pain, but it also forced her to confront her actions. - **Long-term:** If her neglect continues, someone (possibly your brother) could suffer serious harm. Your honesty might have been necessary to prevent that. - **But:** Did you consider whether your approach would *actually* lead to change, or just escalate conflict? 4. **Relational Ethics (How does this affect the relationship?)** - **Trust:** You’ve already been hurt by her (health neglect, financial exploitation). Did you trust her enough to believe she’d respond with openness, or were you operating from a place of betrayal? - **Repair:** Did you leave any space for dialogue, or did you treat her like an opponent rather than a flawed person you still care about? --- ### **Psychological & Emotional Considerations** - **Your Trauma:** You were hospitalized for weeks and spent months recovering. That’s a **legitimate wound**. If she dismisses her role in that, it’s understandable that you’d react with anger. - **Her Reaction:** She cried, felt attacked, and withdrew. This suggests she’s **not ready to hear criticism**—especially not in a way that feels like an accusation of her worth as a mother. - **The Phone Incident:** You were right to protect your brother’s property, but framing it as *"you’re a bad mother"* (even implicitly) may have backfired. She likely felt like you were **generalizing** based on one behavior rather than addressing the specific issue. --- ### **Was It Appropriate? (My Assessment)** **Partially, but with major flaws in execution.** - **What you *should* have done:** - **Separate the person from the behavior.** Instead of saying *"You’re a bad mother,"* try: *"Mom, I know you’re doing your best, but when you ignore doctors like this, it puts us at risk. I need you to take this seriously."* *"I get that you’re frustrated about the phone, but this isn’t about you—it’s about respecting my brother’s things."* - **Acknowledge her feelings.** Even if she’s wrong, her emotions are real. Saying *"I’m not trying to be mean"* is better than *"You’re a bad mother,"* but you could’ve gone further: *"I know this hurts, but I need you to hear this because I care about you."* - **Give her a chance to respond.** Instead of walking away after she cried, you could’ve said: *"I’m not saying this to hurt you. I just need you to know how serious this is."* - **What you *did* do:** - **Directly attacked her identity** (calling her a "bad mother")—this shuts down dialogue. - **Escalated emotionally** (yelling, ultimatums) rather than de-escalating. - **Didn’t leave room for repair.** She needed to feel heard, not judged. --- ### **Why Your Family Might Be Criticizing You** They likely see: - **A child who’s been hurt** (understandably angry). - **A child who’s not yet learned how to have hard conversations without destroying trust.** - **A child who may be repeating patterns** (if she’s dismissive of her own feelings, you might be too). --- ### **Final Verdict: <0 or 1>** **I’d give this a 0.5/1.** - **0.5:** You were **right to speak up** about serious issues (health neglect, financial exploitation). You had every right to protect yourself and your brother. - **0.5:** But **how you said it was deeply flawed**. You could’ve been **just as firm, but far more effective**, if you’d framed it as *"I need you to change this behavior"* rather than *"You’re a bad mother."* --- ### **What Now?** 1. **Repair the Relationship (If You Want To)** - If you still care about her, **reach out with humility**. Say: *"I love you, and I shouldn’t have said those things. I was hurt and scared, but I didn’t mean to make you feel like I didn’t love you too."* - **Ask for forgiveness**, but also **reaffirm your boundaries**: *"I need you to take my health seriously. I need you to respect my brother’s things. I’m not saying this to attack you—I’m saying it because I care."* 2. **Protect Yourself** - If she **continues to neglect your health or exploit you financially**, you may need to **distance yourself** for your own well-being. - **Document incidents** (emails, texts, medical records) in case you need to set firmer boundaries later. 3. **Learn from This** - **Hard conversations require skill.** Next time, **separate the person from the problem**, **acknowledge emotions**, and **focus on solutions**, not blame. - **Trauma changes how we communicate.** If you’re still processing your own health struggles, consider therapy to help you express yourself without escalating conflict. --- ### **Final Thought** You were **right to speak up**, but **wrong in how you did it**. The difference between a **healthy confrontation** and a **toxic one** is often in the **words you choose** and the **intent behind them**. You didn’t have to be cruel to be courageous. Would you say your goal was to **change her behavior** or to **punish her for past hurts**? That might help clarify whether your approach was justified.
